mainTopic: Splitting testimony, punishing עדים זוממין, and the court size for מלקות
overview: The amud opens with more rulings from רבא about witnesses. A husband who testifies that a man sinned with his wife is accepted against the man but not against his wife, because we split a testimony. רבא then rules that עדים זוממין are both executed and made to pay when their lie would have hurt two different people, as when they name the girl's father or the ox's owner. רבא also asks, and then answers, whether a man can testify about his own ox: a person counts as his own relative, but not as a relative to his property. The גמרא then turns to the משנה's rule that lashes need three judges, and רב הונא learns it from the plural word ״וּשְׁפָטוּם״. Along the way, עולא shows that the Torah hints that עדים זוממין receive מלקות, since ״לא תענה״ alone cannot bring lashes. Finally, the גמרא gives two sources for רבי ישמעאל's view that lashes need twenty-three judges: אביי's גזירה שוה on the word ״רשע״, and רבא's idea that lashes stand in place of death. רב אחא בריה דרבא begins challenging רבא's idea, and that discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A husband testifies against the man who sinned with his wife
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that a husband who says 'so-and-so had relations with my wife' counts as a witness against the man, but not against his wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a man says, 'So-and-so had relations with my wife,' he and one more witness can join together to have that man executed, but not to have his wife executed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues a list of rulings from רבא. Here a husband testifies about his own wife's sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A husband may not testify about his wife, because she counts as his close relative. רבא says we do not throw out his whole testimony. We accept the part about the other man, so with one more witness that man can be executed, and we ignore the part about the wife.

keyTerms.meaning: So-and-so; a specific person who is not named
They combine; two witnesses join together to make full testimony

phrases.english: "So-and-so had relations with my wife,"
he and another witness combine to execute him,
but not to execute her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבא's earlier rulings about splitting a testimony
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The husband's testimony is accepted against the other man but not against his wife.

steps.title: Why is this ruling needed if we already split testimony?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what this ruling adds, since splitting a testimony was already taught in the earlier case.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does this teach us? That we split a person's statement? That is the same idea as the earlier case!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's ruling as repetitive. The idea of splitting testimony was already taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier case, a man testified about something done to himself. We accepted his words about the other man and ignored his words about himself. That is the same method as here, so this new ruling seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it teaching us? (asks what a ruling adds)
We split a statement; we accept part of a testimony and reject part
This is the same as that

phrases.english: What is this teaching us?
That we split a statement?
That is the same as that!
phrases.notes: "That" is רבא's earlier case, where a man testified about something done to himself and we split his testimony.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the ruling in step 1
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling about the husband's testimony
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Splitting a testimony was already taught in the earlier self-testimony case, so this ruling seems repetitive.

steps.title: Splitting works for a wife too, not only for oneself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that we might have thought splitting a testimony only works when the witness speaks about himself, not about his wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: when a person speaks about himself, we say 'a person is a relative to himself' and split his words. But when he speaks about his wife, we do not split. So רבא teaches that we split here too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the second ruling is needed after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule אדם קרוב אצל עצמו is what allowed splitting in the earlier case. Someone could think this only applies to a person and himself. They might think a testimony about one's wife must be accepted or rejected as a whole. רבא's ruling shows that splitting applies to the wife as well.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces a mistaken idea we need to rule out)
A person is a relative to himself, so he cannot testify about himself

steps.whatToRemember: We split a testimony and accept the valid part both when a witness speaks about himself and when he speaks about his wife.

phrases.english: You might have said:
"a person is a relative to himself": that we say,
regarding his wife, we do not say it.
So it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 2
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rules out a mistaken idea (מהו דתימא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Splitting works only when the witness speaks about himself, not about his wife.
steps.terutzMaskana: Splitting also works for testimony about one's wife.

steps.title: Plotting witnesses about a betrothed girl: when they also pay
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that עדים זוממין who accuse someone of sinning with a נערה המאורסה are executed. They also pay money only if they named whose daughter she was.
steps.simpleTranslation: If witnesses say 'so-and-so had relations with a betrothed girl' and are proven זוממין, they are executed but do not pay money. If they said 'the daughter of so-and-so' and are proven זוממין, they are executed and also pay money, because the money is for one person and the death penalty is for another.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new ruling about lying witnesses who are caught through הזמה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, one wrongful act gets only one punishment, not both death and payment. But when the witnesses named the girl's father, their lie would have caused a money loss to him and death to the accused. Because there are two separate victims, they get both punishments. If no girl was named, there is no specific person who would have lost money, so they are only executed.

keyTerms.meaning: They were proven to be עדים זוממין (lying witnesses caught by other witnesses)
Money to this one and lives to that one; two different victims

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the rule that עדים זוממין can get two punishments when their lie would have hurt two different people.

phrases.english: And רבא said:
"So-and-so had relations with a betrothed young girl,"
and they were proven plotting witnesses: they are executed,
and they do not pay money.
"the daughter of so-and-so," and they were proven plotting witnesses:
they are executed and they pay money.
Money to this one and lives to that one.
phrases.notes: The money goes to the girl's father. The death penalty matches what they tried to do to the accused.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling from רבא on a different topic: punishing עדים זוממין
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the girl was not named, the זוממין are executed only. If they named her father, they are executed and also pay, because there are two separate victims.

steps.title: Plotting witnesses about an ox: when they also pay
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a parallel ruling: עדים זוממין who accuse someone of bestiality are executed. They also pay for the ox only if they named whose ox it was.
steps.simpleTranslation: If witnesses say 'so-and-so had relations with an ox' and are proven זוממין, they are executed but do not pay money. If they said 'so-and-so's ox' and are proven זוממין, they are executed and also pay money, because the money is for one person and the death penalty is for another.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second case that works exactly like the one before it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The animal involved in such a sin is also put to death, so naming an owner means their lie would have cost him his ox. Since the owner and the accused are two different victims, the witnesses pay and are also executed. With no ox named, no specific owner would have lost anything, so they are only executed.

keyTerms.meaning: So-and-so's ox (a specific owner is named)

steps.whatToRemember: עדים זוממין get both death and payment only when there are two different victims: one who would lose money and one who would lose his life.

phrases.english: And רבא said:
"So-and-so had relations with the ox"
and they were proven plotting witnesses: they are executed,
and they do not pay money.
"so-and-so's ox," and they were proven plotting witnesses:
they are executed, and they pay money.
Money to this one, and lives to that one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel case following the same principle as step 4
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If no ox was named, the זוממין are executed only. If they named the owner, they are executed and also pay, because there are two separate victims.

steps.title: Why do we need the ox case too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבא gave the ox case, since it seems to teach the same thing as the נערה המאורסה case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need this case as well? It is the same as that one!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that רבא's two rulings about עדים זוממין look like the same lesson, so the second one seems unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases the witnesses are executed. They pay money only if they named the owner of the daughter or of the ox. The ox ruling seems to add nothing new to the נערה המאורסה ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: this is the same as that

phrases.english: Why do I also need this one?
phrases.notes: "This one" is the ox case from Step 5, and "that" in the next line is the נערה המאורסה case from Step 4.

phrases.english: This is the same as that!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא תּוּ לְמָה לִי? הַיְינוּ הָךְ!
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether Step 5 is needed after Step 4.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both rulings follow the same pattern, so the second seems repetitive.

steps.title: The ox case sets up a question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבא gave the ox case because he wanted to raise a question about it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he raises a question about it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ox case is needed as a starting point for a question. This line is setting up the next step, where we hear the question itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox case is not there to teach a new rule about עדים זוממין. It sets the scene for a separate question about a man testifying about his own ox.

phrases.english: Because he wants to raise a question about it,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The case is needed as a base for a further question
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ox case only repeats the נערה המאורסה case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ox case is the starting point for רבא's question.

steps.title: Can a man testify about his own ox?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks about a man who says someone had relations with his ox. Is he like a relative to his own property, which would disqualify him?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: if a man says, 'So-and-so had relations with my ox,' what is the law? Do we say a person counts as a relative to himself but not to his property? Or do we say a person counts as a relative to his property too?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks whether a man's testimony about his own ox is accepted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already know a man cannot testify about himself, because he counts as his own relative. The question is whether his property counts as part of 'himself.' If it does not, his testimony about the ox is valid. If it does, his testimony about the ox is rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: a person counts as a relative to himself

phrases.english: As רבא asked:
"So-and-so had relations with my ox" — what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן: אָדָם קָרוֹב אֵצֶל עַצְמוֹ,
phrases.english: Do we say: a person is a relative to himself,
phrases.notes: Relatives can't testify. So calling a person his own "relative" means he can't testify about himself.

phrases.english: but a person is not a relative to his property?
Or perhaps we say:
a person is a relative to his property?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the question that Step 7 said the ox case was needed for.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a person count as a relative to his own property, so that he cannot testify about it?

steps.title: רבא answers: property does not count as oneself
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers his own question: a person counts as his own relative, but not as a relative to his property.
steps.simpleTranslation: After he asked it, he answered it himself: a person is a relative to himself, but a person is not a relative to his property.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers his own question and rules that a man may testify about his own ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the man himself is disqualified, not his belongings. In ״פלוני רבע שורי״ he says nothing about his own sin, only about another man and his own ox. Since his ox does not count as 'himself,' nothing has to be split off: his whole testimony is accepted, and the ox is put to death too.
steps.whatToRemember: A person cannot testify about himself, but he can testify about his property.

phrases.english: After he asked it, he went back and resolved it:
A person is a relative to himself,
but a person is not a relative to his property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A person is not a relative to his property, so his testimony about his ox is accepted.

steps.title: Where do we learn that lashes need three judges?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that lashes are judged by three, and asks for its source.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said that lashes are judged by three judges. From where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic. It quotes the משנה and asks where in the Torah its rule comes from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says a case that could end in מלקות needs a court of three. The גמרא wants a פסוק behind that number.

keyTerms.meaning: etc., the rest of the quote
from where do we know these things?

phrases.english: Lashes are by three, etc.
From where are these words derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, going back to the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The Torah source for having three judges in cases of lashes.

steps.title: רב הונא learns three from ״וּשְׁפָטוּם״
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא says the plural word ״וּשְׁפָטוּם״ means two judges. Since a court can't be even, we add one, making three.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: the verse says 'and they shall judge them,' which means two. A court cannot have an even number, so we add one more. That makes three.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives the source for three judges: a plural word in the פסוק, plus the rule that a court must have an odd number.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plural verb means at least two judges. A court of two could split evenly, so a third is added to break a tie. This gives the משנה's three.

phrases.english: רב הונא said:
The verse says "and they shall judge them" — that is two,
phrases.notes: דברים 25:1. The word is plural, so it means at least two judges.

phrases.english: and a court may not be evenly numbered,
so we add one more to them.
So here there are three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The plural ״וּשְׁפָטוּם״ means two, plus one more to avoid an even court, which makes three.

steps.title: Then the other plural words should give seven
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב הונא: by his logic, ״וְהִצְדִּיקוּ״ and ״וְהִרְשִׁיעוּ״ should each add two more judges, for seven in total.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, 'and they shall justify' is two more, and 'and they shall condemn' is two more. Then there should be seven!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes רב הונא's method further and shows it seems to lead to the wrong number.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every plural verb adds two judges, the same פסוק has two more plural verbs. That would make seven judges, but the משנה says three. So the method seems to prove too much.

keyTerms.meaning: but according to this, if so

phrases.english: But according to this,
"and they shall justify" — two,
"and they shall condemn" — two,
so here there are seven?
phrases.notes: Two plus two plus two makes six, and then one more is added so the court isn't even.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב הונא's method from Step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's method of counting plural verbs
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Applied the same way, the other plural verbs would require seven judges, not three.

steps.title: Those words are needed for עולא's teaching
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that ״וְהִצְדִּיקוּ״ and ״וְהִרְשִׁיעוּ״ are used for a different lesson, from עולא, about a hint for עדים זוממין.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is needed for עולא's teaching, as עולא said: where is there a hint in the Torah for עדים זוממין?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says the extra plural words are used for another lesson, so they cannot be counted as more judges. It begins quoting עולא, and this sets up the next moves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A word that is already used for one lesson is not used to count judges. רב הונא counts only ״וּשְׁפָטוּם״, because the other words are taken up by עולא's teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: witnesses proven to be plotting liars

phrases.english: He needs that for the teaching of עולא,
as עולא said:

phrases.aramaic: רֶמֶז לְעֵדִים זוֹמְמִין מִן הַתּוֹרָה מִנַּיִן?
phrases.english: From where is there a hint in the Torah for עדים זוממין?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The extra words are used for a different lesson
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every plural verb in the פסוק adds two judges.
steps.terutzMaskana: The words ״וְהִצְדִּיקוּ״ and ״וְהִרְשִׁיעוּ״ are used for עולא's teaching, so they don't add judges.

steps.title: עדים זוממין are written openly in the Torah
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why עולא needs a hint for עדים זוממין, since the Torah says it clearly: ״כַּאֲשֶׁר זָמַם״.
steps.simpleTranslation: A hint for עדים זוממין?! But it is clearly written: 'as he plotted'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to question how עולא's words could mean what they seem to say. There is no need for a hint when the Torah states the law of עדים זוממין openly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah openly tells us to punish lying witnesses with what they plotted. So looking for a 'hint' to the basic law makes no sense. עולא must have meant something more specific.

phrases.english: A hint for עדים זוממין?!
But it is written: "as he plotted"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of עולא's statement quoted in Step 13.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The law of עדים זוממין is stated openly, so no hint is needed.

steps.title: The hint is that עדים זוממין get lashes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that עולא was looking for a hint that עדים זוממין receive lashes. He finds it in ״וְהִצְדִּיקוּ אֶת הַצַּדִּיק וְהִרְשִׁיעוּ אֶת הָרָשָׁע״.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, where is there a hint that עדים זוממין receive lashes? As it is written: 'And they shall justify the righteous and condemn the wicked.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא re-reads עולא's question. He meant the special case where עדים זוממין receive מלקות, and he brings the פסוק that hints to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The basic law of הזמה is clear, but lashes for עדים זוממין need a source. עולא finds it in the words ״וְהִצְדִּיקוּ״ and ״וְהִרְשִׁיעוּ״. That is why those words cannot be used to count more judges for רב הונא.
steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא counts only ״וּשְׁפָטוּם״ for three judges, because ״וְהִצְדִּיקוּ״ and ״וְהִרְשִׁיעוּ״ are used for עולא's hint that עדים זוממין receive lashes.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, רֶמֶז לְעֵדִים זוֹמְמִין שֶׁלּוֹקִין מִנַּיִין?
phrases.english: Rather: from where is there a hint that עדים זוממין receive lashes?
As it is written:
"And they shall justify the righteous and condemn the wicked."
phrases.notes: דברים 25:1. The very next פסוק goes on to talk about giving lashes to the guilty one.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, רֶמֶז לְעֵדִים זוֹמְמִין שֶׁלּוֹקִין מִנַּיִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 14 by re-reading עולא's question.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the statement to mean something narrower
steps.terutzHavaAmina: עולא was looking for a hint to the basic law of עדים זוממין.
steps.terutzMaskana: עולא was looking for a hint that עדים זוממין receive lashes, and found it in ״וְהִצְדִּיקוּ״ and ״וְהִרְשִׁיעוּ״.

steps.title: Why would a money case lead to lashes?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: just because one side wins and the other loses, why should the loser get lashes?
steps.simpleTranslation: Just because the judges "justify the righteous and condemn the wicked," does that mean "if the wicked one deserves to be beaten"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the simple reading of the פסוק does not make sense. It is setting up its explanation of how עולא finds a hint for מלקות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the פסוק were about an ordinary court case, losing it is no reason to be whipped. So the next words, about lashes for the רשע, must be about some other situation.

keyTerms.meaning: They declared someone innocent (in the right)
They declared someone guilty (in the wrong)
Deserving to be beaten, meaning deserving lashes

phrases.english: Because "they justified the righteous one
and condemned the wicked one,"
does that mean "and it shall be, if the wicked one deserves to be beaten"?
phrases.notes: דברים 25:2. This is the very next פסוק.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּ״הִצְדִּיקוּ אֶת הַצַּדִּיק וְהִרְשִׁיעוּ אֶת הָרָשָׁע״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the פסוק quoted in Step 15 hints at lashes for עדים זוממין.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How can the פסוק about lashes connect to a simple case where one side wins and one side loses?

steps.title: The verse is about lying witnesses who were caught
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק is about false witnesses who are proven to be עדים זוממין. They become the "רשע" who gets lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: witnesses made an innocent man look guilty. Then other witnesses came and showed he was innocent all along, and made the first witnesses wicked. Of them it says, "if the wicked one deserves to be beaten."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question. The פסוק is talking about lying witnesses who were caught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The "righteous one" is the man the first witnesses falsely accused. The second witnesses prove he was innocent, and that turns the first witnesses into the "wicked." Those witnesses are the ones who get lashes. This is עולא's hint that עדים זוממין receive מלקות.

keyTerms.meaning: Other witnesses (the ones who expose the first pair)
They made them, they turned them into

steps.whatToRemember: According to עולא, ״והיה אם בן הכות הרשע״ refers to עדים זוממין. That is the hint that they get מלקות.

phrases.english: Rather, witnesses who made the righteous one guilty,
and other witnesses came
and showed that the man who was righteous from the start was innocent,
and made those first witnesses into wicked ones,
then "it shall be, if the wicked one deserves to be beaten."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 16 by reading the פסוק as being about witnesses.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק describes עדים זוממין who become "wicked" once other witnesses prove the accused was innocent, so they deserve lashes.

steps.title: Why not learn lashes from "You shall not testify"?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: there is already a לאו against false testimony, so why do we need this hint for lashes?
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him learn it from "You shall not testify falsely"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why עולא needs a special hint. The עשרת הדברות already forbid false testimony, and breaking a לאו usually brings lashes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual rule is that breaking a לאו brings מלקות. Since ״לא תענה״ is a לאו, it looks like it should be enough to give the lying witnesses lashes.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him derive it from (why not just learn it from...)
"You shall not testify" falsely: the prohibition on false testimony

phrases.english: But let him derive it from "You shall not testify"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the hint found in Steps 15-17 is needed at all.
steps.kashyaTarget: עולא's need for a special hint that עדים זוממין get lashes
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A regular לאו already brings lashes, and ״לא תענה״ is a לאו, so a special hint seems unnecessary.

steps.title: No lashes for a prohibition without an action
steps.stepSummary: ״לא תענה״ is a לאו שאין בו מעשה, a prohibition broken without any action, and such a לאו does not bring lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it is a prohibition that involves no action, and for any prohibition that involves no action, we do not give lashes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that ״לא תענה״ cannot bring lashes on its own. Testifying is only speaking, not doing an action.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a rule that you only get מלקות for a לאו you break through an action. False testimony is just talking, so the regular rule cannot give lashes. That is why עולא needed a special hint from the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: A prohibition that you break without doing any physical action

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule, that a לאו שאין בו מעשה does not bring lashes, is a general principle that appears in many places in ש״ס.

phrases.english: Because it is
a prohibition that involves no action,
and for any prohibition that involves no action,
one does not receive lashes for it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּהָוֵה לֵיהּ לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the general rule: the לאו exists, but it cannot bring lashes.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought ״לא תענה״ alone would bring lashes, like any לאו.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because no action is done, ״לא תענה״ cannot bring lashes, so a separate hint is needed.

steps.title: What is רבי ישמעאל's reason for twenty-three judges?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה that, according to רבי ישמעאל, lashes need twenty-three judges, and asks for his reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the name of רבי ישמעאל they said: lashes are judged by twenty-three. What is רבי ישמעאל's reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic in the משנה: רבי ישמעאל's view about the size of the court for lashes. It asks for the source, and the next steps will answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא said lashes need only three judges. רבי ישמעאל requires twenty-three, the size of a court for death cases, so the גמרא wants to know why.

keyTerms.meaning: They said in the name of רבי ישמעאל
Twenty-three: the court size used for death penalty cases

phrases.english: In the name of רבי ישמעאל they said:
by twenty-three judges.
What is the reason of רבי ישמעאל?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new discussion. The earlier steps followed the view that lashes need three judges.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for requiring twenty-three judges in cases of lashes.

steps.title: אביי: a גזירה שוה on the word "wicked"
steps.stepSummary: אביי learns from the word ״רשע״, which appears both by lashes and by a murderer who gets death. Just as a death case needs twenty-three, so do lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: we learn "wicked" from "wicked" in the death penalty cases. Here it says, "if the wicked one deserves to be beaten," and there it says, "who is wicked, deserving death." Just as there it is twenty-three, so too here it is twenty-three.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives רבי ישמעאל's source: a גזירה שוה, a link between two פסוקים that use the same word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ״רשע״ is used for someone who gets lashes and also for a murderer who gets death. Because the same word appears in both places, we take the rule of the death case, a court of twenty-three, and apply it to lashes.

keyTerms.meaning: It is learned from (often used for a גזירה שוה)
Those who deserve the death penalty
It is written here... and it is written there: the formula comparing two פסוקים
Just as there... so too here

phrases.english: אביי said: it is learned from "wicked" and "wicked"
from those who deserve death.

phrases.aramaic: כְּתִיב הָכָא: ״וְהָיָה אִם בִּן הַכּוֹת הָרָשָׁע״,
phrases.english: It is written here: "and it shall be, if the wicked one deserves to be beaten,"
and it is written there: "who is wicked, deserving to die."
Just as there it is by twenty-three judges,
so too here it is by twenty-three judges.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the שאלה of Step 20 with a גזירה שוה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה on ״רשע״ links lashes to death cases, so lashes need twenty-three judges.

steps.title: רבא: lashes stand in place of death
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a reason based on logic: מלקות are a replacement for death, so they are judged like death cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: lashes stand in place of death.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different reason for רבי ישמעאל, with no גזירה שוה. Lashes are treated like a stand-in for the death penalty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי needed a link between two פסוקים. רבא says the idea itself is enough: lashes are a kind of replacement for death, so they need a court of twenty-three just like death cases.

phrases.english: רבא said:
Lashes stand in place of death.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: מַלְקוֹת בִּמְקוֹם מִיתָה עוֹמֶדֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to Step 20, different from אביי's in Step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Lashes replace death, so they are judged like death cases, by twenty-three.

steps.title: If lashes are like death, why estimate his strength?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרבא challenges רבא: if lashes replace death, why does the court estimate how many lashes he can survive? Just whip him, and if he dies, he dies.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא son of רבא said to רב אשי: If so, why do I need an estimate? Let him be whipped, and if he dies, let him die!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבא's idea. If lashes were really like a death sentence, the court would not worry about keeping the person alive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before giving lashes, the court estimates how many the person can take without dying. That care shows lashes are not meant to kill. So how can רבא say they stand in place of death?

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if what you said is true)
An estimate: the court's assessment of how many lashes the person can survive

steps.confusionAlert: רבא does not mean that lashes are a death penalty. He means they come in place of one. The קשיא is about how far that comparison can go.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: רב אחא son of רבא said to רב אשי:
If so, why do I need an estimate?
phrases.notes: Before lashes, the court estimates how many the person can take without dying.

phrases.english: Let him be struck, and if he dies, let him die!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's reasoning from Step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's statement that lashes stand in place of death
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The court estimates his strength so that he will not die. That shows lashes are not treated like death, which goes against רבא.

steps.title: The verse says lashes must fall on a living person
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the פסוק ״וְנִקְלָה אָחִיךָ לְעֵינֶיךָ״ teaches that lashes are given to a living person, so we may not whip him until he dies.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The verse says, "Then your brother will be dishonored before your eyes." When you strike, you strike the back of a living person.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers רב אחא's challenge from Step 23. The פסוק itself shows that we must not whip a person to death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אחא asked: if מלקות replace death, why worry whether he survives? The answer is that the תורה calls the person being whipped "your brother," a living person, so the punishment must be given in a way that keeps him alive. This is why the court estimates how much he can take, and רבא's idea can still stand.

keyTerms.meaning: "Then your brother will be dishonored before your eyes" (the פסוק about lashes)
The back of a living person

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רב אשי answering רב אחא בריה דרבא.

phrases.english: The verse states:
"Then your brother will be dishonored before your eyes"
when you strike,
you strike upon the back of a living person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 23 against רבא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Scriptural limit: a פסוק requires the person to stay alive, even though lashes take the place of death.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If lashes replace death, there should be no need to make sure he survives.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק requires that lashes be given to a living person, so the court must estimate what he can survive.

steps.title: A ברייתא about rounding lashes down to eighteen
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא brings a ברייתא: if the court estimated he can take twenty lashes, he gets only a number divisible by three, which is eighteen. This sets up a further challenge.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about what is taught in a ברייתא: If they estimated that he can take twenty, they strike him only with a number of lashes that can be split into threes. How many is that? Eighteen.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא brings a new source to keep pushing against רבא's approach. The גמרא is setting up the next move. The full question continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lashes are given in sets of three, so a person estimated at twenty gets eighteen, the nearest multiple of three below twenty. The ברייתא shows the court lowers the number below what he can take, and רב אחא is about to ask how this fits with lashes being a replacement for death.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא
They estimated him (how many lashes he can survive)

steps.confusionAlert: This step is not the end of the question. The comma after תַּמְנֵי סְרֵי means the challenge continues on the next amud.

phrases.english: But that which is taught in a baraita:
If they assessed him to receive twenty,
they strike him only
with lashes that can be divided into threes.
And how many are they?
Eighteen,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רב אשי's answer, רב אחא brings a ברייתא to open a further challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's view that מלקות replace death, as defended by רב אשי in Step 24.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא rounds the lashes down below what he can survive. The full challenge from this is spelled out in the next lines.
